text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
context: The opening line of Epictetus' handbook. Everything else in Stoic practice follows from sorting life into what we can govern (our judgments, intentions, actions) and what we cannot (other people, reputation, outcomes).
prompt: What are you carrying today that was never yours to control?

text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.
context: The first verse of the Dhammapada, a collection of sayings attributed to the Buddha. It places the mind at the root of experience: the way we habitually think shapes who we become.
prompt: Which thought have you repeated so often that it now feels like a fact?

text: Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves. Ye shall know them by their fruits…
context: From the Sermon on the Mount. The test offered is practical: judge people not by how they present themselves but by what their lives actually produce.
prompt: Whose words do you trust more than their actions — and does that include your own?

text: Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.
context: Epicurus lived with his friends in a community called the Garden. For him, friendship was not an extra in a good life but its foundation.
prompt: Which friendship deserves more of your attention than it has been getting?

text: Thy business is with the action only, never with its fruits; so let not the fruit of action be thy motive, nor be thou to inaction attached.
context: Spoken to the warrior Arjuna, paralysed by doubt before battle. One of the Gita's central teachings: act fully and well, but release your grip on the result.
prompt: Where are you waiting for a guaranteed outcome before you allow yourself to begin?

text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
context: Socrates says this at his trial in Athens, having been offered the chance to live if he stops questioning people. He chooses the examined life, even at the cost of his own.
prompt: What part of your life have you stopped questioning?

text: If I am not for myself, who will be for me? But if I care for myself only, what am I? And if not now, when?
context: A saying of Hillel the Elder, from the Ethics of the Fathers, a Mishnaic collection of rabbinic wisdom. In three short questions it holds self-respect, responsibility to others and urgency together.
prompt: Which of the three questions do you most need to hear today?

text: Ready must thou be to burn thyself in thine own flame; how couldst thou become new if thou have not first become ashes!
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Way of the Creating One'
context: Zarathustra speaks to someone setting out on their own path. Real renewal asks us to let an old self burn away.
prompt: What old version of yourself might need to become ashes?

text: So, verily, with every difficulty, there is relief: Verily, with every difficulty there is relief.
context: From Surah Ash-Sharh ('The Opening Up'), an early Meccan chapter traditionally understood as consolation during a time of hardship. The line is repeated for emphasis: ease comes with difficulty, not merely after it.
prompt: What relief might already be present inside the difficulty you are facing?

text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.
context: Epictetus, born a slave, taught that suffering often lives in our interpretation of events rather than in the events themselves. Change the judgment and the disturbance changes with it.
prompt: What story are you telling yourself about something that upset you recently?

text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
context: Presented not as a new commandment but as an 'old rule', a law of how things work. Answering hostility with hostility only feeds the cycle.
prompt: Is there a resentment you are keeping alive by feeding it?

text: And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?
context: Also from the Sermon on the Mount. A 'mote' is a speck of dust, a 'beam' a wooden plank. The image is deliberately absurd: we see small faults in others while missing large ones in ourselves.
prompt: What do you criticise in others that you might also find in yourself?

text: Death, therefore, the most awful of evils, is nothing to us, seeing that, when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not.
context: Epicurus wanted to free people from the fear of death, which he saw as poisoning ordinary life. Where we are, death is not; where death is, we are not.
prompt: If fear of an ending were set aside, how would you spend this day?

text: The contacts of matter, O son of Kuntî, giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, they come and go, impermanent; endure them bravely, O Bhârata.
context: Arjuna is reminded that sensations and moods arise and pass like the seasons. Steadiness comes from not mistaking a passing state for the whole of who we are.
prompt: Which feeling right now would you hold more lightly if you remembered it will pass?

text: He knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.
context: Socrates explains why the oracle called him the wisest man in Athens: not because he knew more, but because he was honest about the limits of what he knew.
prompt: Where are you most certain — and what would it cost to be less so?

text: Who is wise? He who learns from all men … Who is mighty? He who controls his passions … Who is rich? He who rejoices in his portion … Who is honored? He who honors others.
context: A teaching of Ben Zoma. Each question takes a quality people chase from the outside and relocates it inside a person's own conduct.
prompt: By which of these four measures do you feel richest today?

text: One must still have chaos in one, to give birth to a dancing star.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue 5
context: Zarathustra warns against a life made so comfortable and orderly that nothing new can arise from it. Inner turmoil can be the raw material of creation.
prompt: What unsettled part of you might be the beginning of something?

text: Nor can goodness and Evil be equal. Repel (Evil) with what is better: Then will he between whom and thee was hatred become as it were thy friend and intimate!
context: From Surah Fussilat. The verse asks for more than restraint: respond to harm with something better, and enmity may turn into closeness.
prompt: Who could you answer with something better than they gave you?

text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial.
context: Written by a Roman emperor in a private notebook. Not cynicism but preparation: he goes on to say such people act from ignorance, and that he cannot be harmed by them or angry with his own kin.
prompt: Who might test your patience today, and how do you want to meet them?

text: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
context: Praise and blame are counted among the 'eight worldly winds' in Buddhist teaching, along with gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain. The wise remain steady in all of them.
prompt: How much of your mood today depends on what others think of you?

text: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
context: Closing a passage on anxiety in the Sermon on the Mount. Each day has enough trouble of its own; borrowing tomorrow's only doubles the weight.
prompt: What worry belongs to tomorrow that you could set down for today?

text: Let no one be slow to seek wisdom when he is young nor weary in the search thereof when he is grown old. For no age is too early or too late for the health of the soul.
context: The opening of Epicurus' letter summarising his ethics. Philosophy, for him, was a lifelong practice of caring for the soul, never too early and never too late.
prompt: What are you still curious to learn about how to live?

text: Better one's own duty, though destitute of merit, than the duty of another, well discharged.
context: The Gita's idea of svadharma: each person has their own path. Living one's own life imperfectly is better than imitating someone else's perfectly.
prompt: Whose life have you been measuring yours against?

text: The beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed and the desired impression is more readily taken.
context: Said in a discussion of how to educate the young: early impressions shape everything that follows. The point applies just as well to habits, projects and days.
prompt: How do you want to begin what comes next?

text: It is not thy duty to complete the work, but neither art thou free to desist from it.
context: A saying of Rabbi Tarfon. The work of repairing the world is too large for one person, but that is no excuse for not doing your part.
prompt: What unfinished work is still worth your small contribution today?

text: Above all, don’t lie to yourself. The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 2
context: Advice from the elder Zosima. Dostoevsky is often read as a forerunner of existentialism for his focus on freedom, conscience and self-deception.
prompt: What small lie have you been telling yourself?

text: No man is a true believer unless he desireth for his brother that which he desireth for himself.
context: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, included in an-Nawawi's classic collection of forty core hadith. It is often compared with the Golden Rule found across many traditions.
prompt: What do you want for yourself that you could also want for someone else?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong-doer.
context: One of the shortest entries in the Meditations. Being wronged offers a choice: to copy the wrong, or to remain who you are.
prompt: Has someone's behaviour been quietly changing yours?

text: If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.
context: From the chapter on 'thousands'. Mastery of one's own mind is placed above any outward victory.
prompt: What small inner victory would matter most today?

text: And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.
context: Luke's version of the Golden Rule, from the Sermon on the Plain. Its phrasing is active: not only avoiding harm, but doing the good you would hope to receive.
prompt: What kindness would you like to receive — and could you offer it first?

text: Nature’s wealth at once has its bounds and is easy to procure; but the wealth of vain fancies recedes to an infinite distance.
context: Natural needs are few and easily met. Desires born of imagination keep moving out of reach however much we acquire.
prompt: Which of your wants keeps receding the closer you get?

text: Let him raise the self by the Self and not let the self become depressed; for verily is the Self the friend of the self, and also the Self the self's enemy.
context: We are asked to lift ourselves up through our own effort. The same mind that can drag us down can also be our closest ally.
prompt: Have you been your own friend or your own enemy this week?

text: Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
context: Socrates says this to the young Theaetetus, who admits he is dizzy with puzzlement. Confusion is not a failure; it is where real thinking starts.
prompt: What has made you wonder recently?

text: A soft answer turneth away wrath; But a grievous word stirreth up anger.
context: From the Book of Proverbs, a collection of practical wisdom in the Hebrew Bible traditionally attributed to King Solomon.
prompt: Where could a gentler word change the course of a conversation?

text: All the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.
context: Pascal, a 17th-century mathematician and religious thinker, anticipated the existentialists' focus on restlessness and distraction.
prompt: Could you sit quietly, alone, for ten minutes today?

text: He is not strong and powerful, who throweth people down; but he is strong who withholdeth himself from anger.
context: A saying of the Prophet Muhammad that redefines strength as self-command rather than force.
prompt: When did you last show strength by holding something back?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it … we do not receive a short life, but we make it a short one, and we are not poor in days, but wasteful of them.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 1
context: Seneca wrote this essay to his friend Paulinus. Life, he argues, is long enough if we know how to use it; it only feels short because we give so much of it away.
prompt: Where did your time go yesterday, and was it given or taken?

text: Let no man think lightly of evil, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little.
context: The verse that follows makes the same point about good. Character is built drop by drop, through small acts we hardly notice.
prompt: What small habit is slowly filling your pot?

text: …let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
context: The Letter of James is the most practical book of the New Testament, close in spirit to the wisdom literature. This line is a whole ethic of conversation in nine words.
prompt: In your next conversation, what would it take to listen first?

text:
'Tis sweet, when, down the mighty main, the winds
Roll up its waste of waters, from the land
To watch another's labouring anguish far,
Not that we joyously delight that man
Should thus be smitten, but because 'tis sweet
To mark what evils we ourselves be spared;
'Tis sweet, again, to view the mighty strife
Of armies embattled yonder o'er the plains,
Ourselves no sharers in the peril; but naught
There is more goodly than to hold the high
Serene plateaus, well fortressed by the wise,
Whence thou may'st look below on other men
And see them ev'rywhere wand'ring, all dispersed
In their lone seeking for the road of life.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius, a Roman poet, set Epicurus' philosophy to verse. Here he describes the calm of a mind that has found its footing, looking out on a restless world.
prompt: Where is your 'serene plateau' when life gets stormy?

text: The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man. It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end. The good and the pleasant approach man: the wise goes round about them and distinguishes them. Yea, the wise prefers the good to the pleasant, but the fool chooses the pleasant through greed and avarice.
context: Spoken by Death to the young seeker Nachiketas, who has refused every pleasure offered him in exchange for real understanding.
prompt: Where are the good and the pleasant pulling you in different directions?

text: Then would you rather suffer than do injustice? — I should not like either, but if I must choose between them, I would rather suffer than do.
context: Socrates shocks his companions by arguing that doing wrong damages the soul far more than being wronged does.
prompt: Is there a wrong you could avoid doing, even at some cost to yourself?

text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
context: From Kohelet (Ecclesiastes), the Hebrew Bible's most philosophical book. It continues: a time to plant and a time to uproot, a time to weep and a time to laugh.
prompt: What season of life are you in right now?

text: In one’s friend one shall have one’s best enemy. Thou shalt be closest unto him with thy heart when thou withstandest him.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Friend'
context: For Nietzsche, a true friend challenges us rather than flatters us, and we are closest to them when we push back.
prompt: Which friend challenges you, and do you challenge them?

text: Nor walk on the earth with insolence: for thou canst not rend the earth asunder, nor reach the mountains in height.
context: From Surah Al-Isra, in a passage of ethical guidance. The image puts arrogance in proportion: however proud our stride, the earth and the mountains are larger.
prompt: Where might a little more humility lighten your step?

text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, sea-shores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself.
context: Marcus reminds himself that the quiet he longs for in the countryside is always available within. The retreat is a practice, not a place.
prompt: Where in yourself can you retreat to, right now, for a minute?

text: He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"—in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease. "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me,"—in those who do not harbour such thoughts hatred will cease."
context: Two nearly identical verses that differ by a single word. Hatred lives on in the stories we rehearse about the wrongs done to us.
prompt: Which old grievance do you still replay, and what would happen if you stopped?

text: Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
context: Said to ordinary listeners, not to the powerful. What is good in a person is meant to be seen, not hidden away.
prompt: What good in you have you been keeping out of sight?

text: Accustom thyself to believe that death is nothing to us, for good and evil imply sentience, and death is the privation of all sentience; therefore a right understanding that death is nothing to us makes the mortality of life enjoyable, not by adding to life an illimitable time, but by taking away the yearning after immortality.
context: The goal is not to make life longer but to make mortal life enjoyable, by letting go of the craving to live forever.
prompt: How would you live if you made peace with being mortal?

text: As a man, casting off worn-out garments, taketh new ones, so the dweller in the body, casting off worn-out bodies, entereth into others that are new.
context: The Gita teaches that the deepest self is not destroyed with the body. Whatever one believes about rebirth, the image invites us to see change as renewal.
prompt: What 'worn-out garment' in your life are you ready to lay aside?

text: Be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
context: Socrates' words to the jurors who voted to acquit him. A good person's integrity cannot be taken from them by anything that happens.
prompt: What in you can no misfortune touch?

text: Say little and do much; and receive all men with a cheerful countenance.
context: A saying of Shammai, Hillel's famously strict counterpart. Even he counsels warmth: greet everyone with a kind face.
prompt: Who could you greet more warmly today?

text: He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster. And if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 146
context: A warning to anyone fighting something they despise: the struggle can reshape us into what we oppose.
prompt: Is something you are fighting changing you?

text: Actions will be judged according to intentions.
context: Traditionally placed first in the great hadith collections, as the foundation of everything else: the worth of what we do rests on why we do it.
prompt: What is the intention behind what you will do today?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
context: A compressed version of the Stoic method: the injury we feel is bound up with the judgment that we have been injured.
prompt: Which 'I have been harmed' could you set down today?

text: The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once.
context: Remembering that every life ends puts most quarrels in proportion.
prompt: Which disagreement would fade if you remembered how short life is?

text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
context: Our attention and affection follow what we value. Look at where your treasure is, and you will find your heart.
prompt: Judging by where your time and money go, where is your heart?

text: And even as men choose of food not merely and simply the larger portion, but the more pleasant, so the wise seek to enjoy the time which is most pleasant and not merely that which is longest.
context: The quality of a life matters more than its length, just as we choose food for its taste, not its quantity.
prompt: How could you make today sweeter rather than longer?

text: For certain is death for the born, and certain is birth for the dead; therefore over the inevitable thou shouldst not grieve.
context: Not a dismissal of grief, but a reminder that the cycle of life and death is the most certain thing there is.
prompt: What inevitable change are you still resisting?

text: The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.
context: Sentenced to die, Socrates observes that wrongdoing is the swifter pursuer. His accusers, he says, have been overtaken by it.
prompt: What wrong is easier to fall into than you'd like to admit?

text: I have found nothing better for man than silence; not learning but doing is the chief thing; and whoso multiplies words causes sin.
context: A saying of Shimon, son of Rabban Gamaliel. Study matters, but what we do matters more, and too many words lead us astray.
prompt: Where could you replace talking with doing?

text: To "give style" to one's character—that is a grand and a rare art! He who surveys all that his nature presents in its strength and in its weakness, and then fashions it into an ingenious plan, until everything appears artistic and rational, and even the weaknesses enchant the eye—exercises that admirable art.
context: Nietzsche imagines character as a work of art: survey your strengths and weaknesses, and shape them into a whole.
prompt: If your character were a work of art, what would you refine?

text: And be moderate in thy pace, and lower thy voice; for the harshest of sounds without doubt is the braying of the ass.
context: Part of the advice of Luqman, a sage, to his son. A blunt, almost humorous image: loudness is not strength.
prompt: Where could a quieter voice carry more weight?

text: Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
context: The Stoics used the awareness of death not to frighten but to focus: the time to be good is now, while it is still possible.
prompt: What good thing have you been postponing as if you had endless time?

text: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
context: The 'flood' in Buddhist imagery is the rush of craving and confusion. Steady effort builds an island where the mind can stand.
prompt: What practice could be your island this week?

text: Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?
context: A cubit is about half a metre. Worry, the passage says, adds nothing to a life, not even a little.
prompt: What has your worrying actually changed this week?

text: We must remember that the future is neither wholly ours nor wholly not ours, so that neither must we count upon it as quite certain to come nor despair of it as quite certain not to come.
context: A balanced stance toward the future: neither counting on it nor despairing of it.
prompt: What are you either counting on or despairing of too much?

text: He whose mind is free from anxiety amid pains, indifferent amid pleasures, loosed from passion, fear and anger, is called a sage of stable mind.
context: A portrait of the 'sthitaprajna', the person of steady wisdom: undisturbed by pain, unseduced by pleasure, free of fear and anger.
prompt: What unsettles your mind most easily?

text: The hour of departure has arrived, and we go our ways—I to die, and you to live.
context: The final words of Socrates' defence, spoken with calm to the court that has condemned him.
prompt: How would you want to speak if these were your last words?

text: Judge not thy neighbor until thou art come into his place.
context: One of Hillel's best-known teachings. We cannot fairly judge a person whose circumstances we have never stood in.
prompt: Whose place have you never stood in, though you judge them?

text: Amor fati: let that henceforth be my love! I do not want to wage war with the ugly. I do not want to accuse, I do not want even to accuse the accusers. Looking aside, let that be my sole negation! And all in all, to sum up: I wish to be at any time hereafter only a yea-sayer!
context: 'Amor fati' means love of fate. Nietzsche's New Year's resolution: to accept, and even love, what is necessary in his life.
prompt: What in your life could you say 'yes' to, rather than resist?

text: By (the Token of) Time (through the ages), Verily Man is in loss, Except such as have Faith, and do righteous deeds, and (join together) in the mutual teaching of Truth, and of Patience and Constancy.
context: Surah Al-Asr ('Time') in full, one of the shortest chapters. Time is passing for everyone; what redeems it is good deeds and encouraging one another in truth and patience.
prompt: Who encourages you in truth and patience, and whom do you encourage?

text: Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.
context: Marcus quotes Democritus, then refines the advice: do what is necessary, and you gain the calm of doing few things and doing them well.
prompt: What could you stop doing to make room for what matters?

text: As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.
context: A fletcher straightens arrows by patient heating and bending. The mind can be trained the same way.
prompt: Where is your thinking bent today, and how might you straighten it?

text: Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
context: The easy road is crowded; the road that leads to real life is narrow and less travelled.
prompt: Where are you taking the wide road because everyone else is?

text: For the end of all our actions is to be free from pain and fear, and, when once we have attained all this, the tempest of the soul is laid.
context: Epicurus' aim was ataraxia, a calm, untroubled mind. Once it is reached, there is nothing more to chase.
prompt: What is stirring a tempest in your soul right now?

text: Man, musing on the objects of sense, conceiveth an attachment to these; from attachment ariseth desire; from desire anger cometh forth From anger proceedeth delusion; from delusion confused memory; from confused memory the destruction of Reason; from destruction of Reason he perishes.
context: A precise chain of cause and effect: dwelling leads to attachment, attachment to desire, desire to anger, and anger to the loss of clear thinking.
prompt: What have you been dwelling on that could start this chain?

text: I would rather die having spoken after my manner, than speak in your manner and live.
context: Socrates refuses to beg for mercy or bring his weeping children to court. He would rather die true to himself than live by betraying himself.
prompt: Where are you speaking in someone else's manner to stay comfortable?

text: In a place where there are no men, strive to be a man.
context: Another saying of Hillel. When no one else steps up, that is precisely the moment to act with integrity.
prompt: Where is no one stepping up, and could it be you?

text: Thou shalt become what thou art.
context: Nietzsche's answer to the question 'What saith thy conscience?' Borrowed from the Greek poet Pindar, it became his motto.
prompt: Who are you becoming, and is it who you are?

text: The proof of a Muslim's sincerity is that he payeth no heed to that which is not his business.
context: Included in an-Nawawi's forty hadith. Much distraction, and much harm, comes from busying ourselves with what does not concern us.
prompt: What could you let go of because it simply isn't your business?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Be like the promontory against which the waves continually break, but it stands firm and tames the fury of the water around it.
context: An image of steadiness. The waves do not stop coming; the rock simply does not move, and the water around it grows calm.
prompt: What keeps breaking against you, and how could you stand more firmly?

text: It is good to tame the mind, which is difficult to hold in and flighty, rushing wherever it listeth; a tamed mind brings happiness.
context: The untrained mind rushes wherever it likes. Taming it is not suppression but steadiness, and steadiness brings ease.
prompt: Where did your mind rush off to today?

text: Blessed are the meek: for they shall inherit the earth.
context: One of the Beatitudes. 'Meek' here means gentle and self-possessed, not weak: strength that does not need to dominate.
prompt: Where could gentleness be the stronger choice today?

text: We do not choose every pleasure whatsoever, but ofttimes pass over many pleasures when a greater annoyance ensues from them. And ofttimes we consider pains superior to pleasures when submission to the pains for a long time brings us as a consequence a greater pleasure.
context: Epicurus is often mistaken for a hedonist. In fact he taught careful weighing: some pleasures cost too much, some pains are worth it.
prompt: Which pleasure costs you more than it gives?

text: He attaineth Peace, into whom all desires flow as rivers flow into the ocean, which is filled with water, but remaineth unmoved—not he who desireth desires.
context: The ocean receives every river yet stays the same. Peace is not the absence of desires but not being moved by them.
prompt: Which desire could you let flow in without letting it move you?

text: For I do nothing but go about persuading you all, old and young alike, not to take thought for your persons or your properties, but first and chiefly to care about the greatest improvement of the soul. I tell you that virtue is not given by money, but that from virtue comes money and every other good of man, public as well as private.
context: Socrates describes the message he has spent his life repeating to the people of Athens: care first for your soul.
prompt: How much of your care goes to your soul, compared with your possessions?

text: Despise not any man, and carp not at any thing; for there is not a man that has not his hour, and there is not a thing that has not its place.
context: A saying of Ben Azzai. Every person will have their moment, and every thing its use.
prompt: Whom have you underestimated?

text: Build your cities on the slope of Vesuvius! Send your ships into unexplored seas! Live in war with your equals and with yourselves!
context: A provocation against timid, comfortable living. 'Living in war with yourselves' means continual self-challenge, not violence.
prompt: What unexplored sea have you been afraid to sail?

text: Make not thy hand tied (like a niggard's) to thy neck, nor stretch it forth to its utmost reach, so that thou become blameworthy and destitute.
context: A picture of balance in giving: neither a hand chained shut in miserliness nor one stretched so wide that nothing is left.
prompt: Is your hand too closed, or too open, right now?

text: Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
context: Just as cloth takes on the colour it soaks in, the mind takes on the colour of what it repeatedly thinks.
prompt: What colour is your mind being dyed by lately?

text: Not a mother, not a father will do so much, nor any other relative; a well-directed mind will do us greater service.
context: Even the people who love us most cannot do for us what a well-directed mind can.
prompt: What direction would you like to give your mind today?

text: But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth.
context: Generosity that seeks recognition is a kind of trade. The teaching asks for giving so quiet that even you barely notice it.
prompt: What could you give today without anyone knowing?

text: We regard independence of outward things as a great good, not so as in all cases to use little, but so as to be contented with little if we have not much, being honestly persuaded that they have the sweetest enjoyment of luxury who stand least in need of it, and that whatever is natural is easily procured and only the vain and worthless hard to win.
context: The point is not to live with little, but to be able to be content with little, which makes us freer whatever we have.
prompt: What could you happily do without?

text: When, again, as a tortoise draws in on all sides its limbs, he withdraws his senses from the objects of sense, then is his understanding well poised.
context: The tortoise draws in its limbs when it needs to. The wise can likewise withdraw from the pull of the senses at will.
prompt: When did you last withdraw, deliberately, from all the noise?

text: Not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued…
context: In prison, his friend Crito urges Socrates to escape. Socrates insists the question is not how to live longer but how to live well.
prompt: Are you living a long life, or a good one?

text: Look not at the flask, but at what it contains: there may be a new flask full of old wine, and an old flask that has not even new wine in it.
context: A saying of Rabbi Meir. Appearances, including age and youth, tell us little about what is inside.
prompt: Whose 'flask' have you judged without tasting the wine?

text: What dost thou Love in others?—My hopes.
context: One of a series of short questions and answers in which Nietzsche examines himself.
prompt: What do you love in the people closest to you?

text: Be not angry.
context: A man asked the Prophet for advice; the answer was three words. Some traditions add that he asked again and again, and received the same reply.
prompt: What would your day look like if you took this as your only advice?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Let not future things disturb thee, for thou wilt come to them, if it shall be necessary, having with thee the same reason which now thou usest for present things.
context: Anxiety imagines the future without the resources we will actually have when we get there. The same reason that serves us now will serve us then.
prompt: What future worry would feel smaller if you trusted your future self?

text: Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of.
context: A counsel of attention: it is easier to tally the failings of others than to notice our own.
prompt: What would you notice if you looked at your own day the way you look at others'?

text: …be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
context: Said to disciples being sent into a hostile world. Innocence and shrewdness are not opposites; we need both.
prompt: Where do you need to be wiser, without becoming harder?

text: Plain fare gives as much pleasure as a costly diet, when once the pain of want has been removed, while bread and water confer the highest possible pleasure when they are brought to hungry lips.
context: Epicurus' own diet was famously simple. Bread and water, eaten when truly hungry, give the deepest pleasure.
prompt: When did a simple thing last give you real pleasure?

text: Therefore cleave thou to yoga; yoga is skill in action.
context: One of the Gita's most famous definitions. Yoga here is not posture but a way of acting: skilful, balanced and free of grasping.
prompt: What would it mean to act with real skill today?

text: Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to any one, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.
context: Socrates admits this view has never been popular. He holds to it anyway, even facing death.
prompt: Whom are you tempted to repay in kind?

text: He whose wisdom exceeds his works, to what is he like? To a tree whose branches are many, but whose roots are few; and the wind comes and plucks it up, and overturns it upon its face … But he whose works exceed his wisdom, to what is he like? To a tree whose branches are few, but whose roots are many, so that though all the winds in the world come and blow upon it, they cannot stir it from its place.
context: A saying of Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah. Knowledge without deeds is a tree with a large crown and shallow roots.
prompt: Are your roots as deep as your branches are wide?

text: Man is a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman—a rope over an abyss.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue 4
context: Zarathustra speaks to a crowd waiting for a tightrope walker. Human life is a crossing, not a destination.
prompt: What are you crossing toward?

text: Those who spend (freely), whether in prosperity, or in adversity; who restrain anger, and pardon (all) men…
context: A description of the people of good character: generous in good times and bad, holding back anger, forgiving others.
prompt: Which of these three would ask the most of you today?

text: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
context: Goodness is not imported from outside; it is a spring to be uncovered, again and again.
prompt: What good in you needs digging out today?

text: Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.
context: Beautiful words without matching action are like a flower with no scent: lovely to look at, but empty.
prompt: Which of your words are still waiting for their deeds?

text: …for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
context: Speech reveals what fills us. What we say most easily shows what we carry inside.
prompt: What have your words revealed about your heart lately?

text: When we say, then, that pleasure is the end and aim, we do not mean the pleasures of the prodigal or the pleasures of sensuality, as we are understood to do by some through ignorance, prejudice, or wilful misrepresentation. By pleasure we mean the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul.
context: Epicurus corrects the caricature of his teaching. The pleasure he means is the absence of pain and inner trouble.
prompt: What would bring a little more peace to your body and soul today?

text: Nor can anyone, even for an instant, remain really actionless.
context: Even doing nothing is a kind of action. The question is never whether to act, but how.
prompt: What are you 'doing' even when you think you are doing nothing?

text: We must not regard what the many say of us: but what he, the one man who has understanding of just and unjust, will say, and what the truth will say.
context: Public opinion is not the measure of right and wrong. Socrates asks what someone who truly understands would say, and what the truth would say.
prompt: Whose opinion are you living by, the many's or the truth's?

text: Above all that thou guardest keep thy heart; For out of it are the issues of life.
context: The inner life is described as the source from which everything else flows, and so the thing most worth guarding.
prompt: What have you been letting into your heart lately?

text: Flee, my friend, into thy solitude! I see thee deafened with the noise of the great men, and stung all over with the stings of the little ones.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Flies in the Market-place'
context: The market-place is full of noise, fame and petty attacks. Zarathustra urges his friend to recover himself in solitude.
prompt: Which noise could you step away from today?

text: Your smiling in your brother's face, is charity; and your exhorting mankind to virtuous deeds, is charity; and your prohibiting the forbidden, is charity; and your showing men the road, in the land in which they lose it, is charity; and your assisting the blind, is charity.
context: Charity in Islam is not only money. A smile, a kind word, or showing someone the way all count.
prompt: What small charity, costing nothing, could you give today?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgment about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgment now.
context: One of the clearest statements of Stoic freedom: the judgment is ours, so we can revise it, not someday but now.
prompt: Which judgment about your situation could you revise right now?

text: Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.
context: Three images of how time stretches: for the sleepless, the weary, and those who live without understanding.
prompt: What makes your days feel long, and what makes them feel full?

text: For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?
context: A question that measures success against something deeper. Achievement that costs us ourselves is a bad bargain.
prompt: Is there something you are gaining at too high a cost?

text: It is not an unbroken succession of drinking-bouts and of revelry, not sexual love, not the enjoyment of the fish and other delicacies of a luxurious table, which produce a pleasant life; it is sober reasoning, searching out the grounds of every choice and avoidance, and banishing those beliefs through which the greatest tumults take possession of the soul.
context: A pleasant life comes from thinking clearly about what we choose and why, and from letting go of beliefs that disturb us.
prompt: Which of your beliefs causes you the most unrest?

text: Perform thou right action, for, action is superior to inaction.
context: Krishna urges Arjuna out of paralysis. Withdrawal from life is not the answer; right action is.
prompt: Where has hesitation become a kind of inaction?

text: We shall be better and braver and less helpless if we think that we ought to enquire, than we should have been if we indulged in the idle fancy that there was no knowing and no use in seeking to know what we do not know.
context: Socrates is unsure of much, but of this he is certain: believing inquiry is worthwhile makes us better people.
prompt: What question have you given up on that is still worth asking?

text: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; Consider her ways, and be wise.
context: The ant has no overseer, the passage continues, yet it gathers its food in summer. Diligence needs no supervisor.
prompt: What would you do today if no one were checking?

text: And lost be the day to us in which a measure hath not been danced. And false be every truth which hath not had laughter along with it!
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra III, 'Old and New Tables' 23
context: Nietzsche prized joy, lightness and dance as signs of a life fully affirmed.
prompt: When did you last dance or laugh?

text: When a (courteous) greeting is offered you, meet it with a greeting still more courteous, or (at least) of equal courtesy…
context: Courtesy as a practice: answer kindness with a little more kindness.
prompt: How could you return a greeting a little more warmly today?

text: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
context: Marcus, tired of his own philosophising, tells himself to stop describing virtue and start living it.
prompt: What ideal have you been discussing that you could simply live today?

text: These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me," with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?"
context: A reflection on possession: we say 'mine' about people and things, yet we do not even fully own ourselves.
prompt: What do you call 'mine' that you might hold more loosely?

text: …the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
context: Spoken in the garden of Gethsemane to disciples who kept falling asleep. A compassionate recognition of the gap between intention and strength.
prompt: Where are your intentions good but your follow-through tired?

text: Wherefore prudence is a more precious thing even than philosophy; from it spring all the other virtues, for it teaches that we cannot lead a life of pleasure which is not also a life of prudence, honour, and justice; nor lead a life of prudence, honour, and justice, which is not also a life of pleasure. For the virtues have grown into one with a pleasant life, and a pleasant life is inseparable from them.
context: For Epicurus, a pleasant life and a good life are the same thing: you cannot have one without the other.
prompt: Where do pleasure and goodness meet in your life?

text: Whatsoever a great man doeth, that other men also do; the standard he setteth up, by that the people go.
context: Example teaches more than instruction. Those whom others look up to carry a particular responsibility.
prompt: Who is watching how you live, and what are they learning?

text: There is a victory and defeat—the first and best of victories, the lowest and worst of defeats—which each man gains or sustains at the hands, not of another, but of himself; this shows that there is a war against ourselves going on within every one of us.
context: From Plato's last and longest dialogue. The fiercest war is the one fought within each person.
prompt: What inner battle are you fighting right now?

text: Care in the heart of a man boweth it down; But a good word maketh it glad.
context: Anxiety weighs a person down, and a kind word can lift them. A small thing with a large effect.
prompt: Who around you might need a good word today?

text: Of all that is written, I love only what a person hath written with his blood. Write with blood, and thou wilt find that blood is spirit.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'Reading and Writing'
context: Nietzsche valued writing, and living, that come from genuine experience rather than borrowed opinion.
prompt: What could you say, or do, today that comes from your own blood?

text: Riches are not from abundance of worldly goods, but from a contented mind.
context: Wealth is redefined as an inner state: contentment.
prompt: What would make your mind feel rich today?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others.
context: A puzzled observation from the last book of the Meditations: we care most about ourselves, yet trust others' view of us more than our own.
prompt: Whose opinion of you counts for more than your own, and why?

text: The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.
context: Wisdom begins with knowing the limits of one's own understanding.
prompt: Where might you be the fool who thinks himself wise?

text: …The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath.
context: A reply to critics who objected to disciples picking grain on the day of rest. Rules exist to serve human life, not the other way round.
prompt: Which rule in your life has forgotten what it was for?

text: Some things happen of necessity, others by chance, others through our own agency. For he sees that necessity destroys responsibility and that chance or fortune is inconstant; whereas our own actions are free.
context: Against fatalism, Epicurus insists that much of life is up to us. Responsibility depends on it.
prompt: What part of your situation is truly in your own hands?

text: It is desire, it is wrath, begotten by the quality of motion; all-consuming, all-polluting, know thou this as our foe here on earth.
context: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong even against their will. The answer: desire and its companion, anger.
prompt: Where have desire or anger acted through you lately?

text: I would rather that my lyre should be inharmonious, and that there should be no music in the chorus which I provided; aye, or that the whole world should be at odds with me, and oppose me, rather than that I myself should be at odds with myself, and contradict myself.
context: Socrates would rather the whole world disagree with him than live in disagreement with himself.
prompt: Where are you at odds with yourself?

text: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise; But the companion of fools shall smart for it.
context: We become like the company we keep.
prompt: Whose company is shaping you, and in what direction?

text: There is more sagacity in thy body than in thy best wisdom.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra I, 'The Despisers of the Body'
context: Against those who despise the body, Zarathustra insists it holds an intelligence of its own.
prompt: What is your body trying to tell you?

text: But indeed if any show patience and forgive, that would truly be an exercise of courageous will and resolution in the conduct of affairs.
context: Following a verse that permits fair retaliation, this one names something higher: patience and forgiveness as a form of courage.
prompt: Where would forgiving take more courage than retaliating?

text: Every man lives only this present time, which is an indivisible point, and that all the rest of his life is either past or it is uncertain.
context: The past is gone and the future unknown; the only life anyone actually lives is the present moment.
prompt: What would change if you gave this moment your whole attention?

text: If you see an intelligent man who tells you where true treasures are to be found, who shows what is to be avoided, and administers reproofs, follow that wise man; it will be better, not worse, for those who follow him.
context: A person who corrects us honestly is described as someone pointing to buried treasure.
prompt: Who tells you hard truths, and how do you receive them?

text: Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven.
context: The measure we use on others tends to come back to us. Mercy given makes room for mercy received.
prompt: Whom could you stop judging today?

text: Death is nothing to us; for the body, when it has been resolved into its elements, has no feeling, and that which has no feeling is nothing to us.
context: The second of Epicurus' forty core teachings, memorised by his followers. Death cannot harm one who no longer feels.
prompt: What fear might shrink if you looked at it this plainly?

text: Verily there is no purifier in this world like wisdom.
context: Understanding, more than ritual, is what transforms a person.
prompt: What understanding has changed you most?

text: Let us, then, take the argument as our guide, which has revealed to us that the best way of life is to practise justice and every virtue in life and death.
context: The closing words of the Gorgias. After a long and heated argument, Socrates concludes simply: practise justice and every virtue.
prompt: What would it mean to follow the argument wherever it leads?

text: A tranquil heart is the life of the flesh; But envy is the rottenness of the bones.
context: An observation about body and spirit: a calm heart sustains life, while envy eats away at a person from within.
prompt: Is there any envy quietly eating at you?

text: “What is hell?” I maintain that it is the suffering of being unable to love.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 3
context: From the teachings of the elder Zosima, gathered after his death. Hell is not a place but a condition: the loss of the capacity to love.
prompt: Where has your capacity to love grown thin?

text: There are two benefits, of which the generality of men are losers, and of which they do not know the value, health and leisure.
context: Two gifts we usually notice only once they are gone.
prompt: How are you using your health and your free time?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: The perfection of moral character consists in this, in passing every day as the last, and in being neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite.
context: Living each day as if it were the last, in the Stoic sense, means neither frantic nor numb, but awake and sincere.
prompt: If today were your last, what would you stop pretending?

text: Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.
context: Every craft shapes its material. The wise treat their own character as the material to be shaped.
prompt: What part of yourself are you shaping right now?

text: …Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful…
context: Martha is busy serving guests while her sister Mary sits and listens. The gentle rebuke is not against work, but against being scattered.
prompt: Among all the things troubling you, what is the one thing needful?

text: The magnitude of pleasure reaches its limit in the removal of all pain.
context: Pleasure has a ceiling: once pain is gone, more does not mean better. This frees us from chasing endless increase.
prompt: Where are you chasing 'more' past the point of enough?

text: Sages look equally on a Brâhmana adorned with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, and even a dog and an outcaste.
context: A radical statement of equality in its time: the wise see the same essence in a learned priest, an animal and a person society rejects.
prompt: Whom do you find it hardest to see as equal?

text: Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads.
context: The opening of the Allegory of the Cave. Prisoners mistake shadows on a wall for reality; philosophy is the slow, painful turn toward the light.
prompt: What shadows might you be mistaking for the real thing?

text: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, Than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
context: A 'stalled ox' was a fattened animal, a feast. A simple meal among people who love each other is worth more.
prompt: Where is love more present in your life than luxury?

text: Love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4
context: Zosima to a woman who dreams of serving humanity but cannot bear ingratitude. Real love is slow, unglamorous and costly.
prompt: Where is your love still in dreams, and where is it in action?

text: And what will explain to thee the path that is steep?- (It is:) freeing the bondman; Or the giving of food in a day of privation To the orphan with claims of relationship, Or to the indigent (down) in the dust.
context: From Surah Al-Balad. The 'steep path' is not a mystical ascent but practical compassion: freeing the captive, feeding the hungry.
prompt: What would taking the steep path look like for you this week?

text: When thou art offended with any man's shameless conduct, immediately ask thyself, Is it possible, then, that shameless men should not be in the world? It is not possible. Do not, then, require what is impossible.
context: Expecting a world without difficult people only guarantees frustration. Marcus asks himself to expect them, and so to meet them calmly.
prompt: What are you demanding of others that is simply impossible?

text: Wise people, after they have listened to the laws, become serene, like a deep, smooth, and still lake.
context: Understanding, once truly absorbed, does not agitate. It settles the mind like a still lake.
prompt: What would help your mind become a little more still today?

text: …Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
context: Spoken before the parable of the rich fool, who builds bigger barns and dies that night.
prompt: What does your life consist of, if not your possessions?

text: Continuous pain does not last long in the flesh; on the contrary, pain, if extreme, is present a very short time, and even that degree of pain which barely outweighs pleasure in the flesh does not last for many days together.
context: Epicurus himself suffered from painful illness. His teaching was that severe pain is brief and long pain is bearable.
prompt: What pain have you endured that turned out more bearable than you feared?

text: Verily yoga is not for him who eateth too much, nor who abstaineth to excess, nor who is too much addicted to sleep, nor even to wakefulness, O Arjuna. Yoga killeth out all pain for him who is regulated in eating and amusement, regulated in performing actions, regulated in sleeping and waking.
context: The path is one of moderation: neither indulgence nor extreme austerity, in food, sleep, work or play.
prompt: Where in your daily rhythm is balance missing?

text: Wealth, I said, and poverty; the one is the parent of luxury and indolence, and the other of meanness and viciousness, and both of discontent.
context: Socrates names two dangers to a healthy community, and to a healthy soul: too much and too little.
prompt: Has abundance or scarcity been shaping your character lately?

text: Pride goeth before destruction, And a haughty spirit before a fall.
context: One of the most quoted lines of the Hebrew Bible. Arrogance blinds us to the edge we are walking toward.
prompt: Where might pride be blinding you?

text: Every one is really responsible to all men for all men and for everything.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 2
context: Spoken by Zosima's dying brother Markel, who in his last days discovers a joyful sense of connection to everyone.
prompt: What would change if you felt responsible for those around you?

text: When you see a person, who has been given more than you in money and beauty; then look to those who have been given less.
context: A practical cure for envy: whenever you compare yourself upward, also look at those with less.
prompt: Who has less than you, and what does that show you about what you have?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
context: The Stoics saw humans as social by nature. When others fall short, there are only two fitting responses: help them see, or be patient.
prompt: Is there someone you could teach, or someone you need to bear with?

text: Even though a speech be a thousand (of words), but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.
context: Quantity of words is not the measure. One true word that brings peace outweighs a thousand empty ones.
prompt: What one word of sense do you need to hear, or to say?

text: …For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required…
context: Gifts come with responsibility. The more we have received, the more is fairly asked of us.
prompt: What have you been given that asks something of you in return?

text: It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly.
context: Pleasure, wisdom and justice are bound together. None can be had fully without the others.
prompt: Which of the three is weakest in your life right now?

text: As a lamp in a windless place flickereth not, to such is likened the Yogî of subdued thought, absorbed in the yoga of the Self.
context: A classic image of a concentrated mind: a flame so sheltered it does not flicker.
prompt: What winds make your mind flicker?

text: Bodily exercise, when compulsory, does no harm to the body; but knowledge which is acquired under compulsion obtains no hold on the mind. … do not use compulsion, but let early education be a sort of amusement; you will then be better able to find out the natural bent.
context: Plato's view of education: learning forced on us does not last. Learning through play reveals who we really are.
prompt: What would you love to learn if no one were making you?

text: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; And he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
context: Self-mastery is ranked above military conquest. Ruling one's own spirit is the harder victory.
prompt: What part of your spirit needs ruling today?

text: There is nothing higher and stronger and more wholesome and good for life in the future than some good memory, especially a memory of childhood, of home. source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Epilogue, ch. 3
context: Alyosha's speech to a group of boys at the funeral of their friend. Good memories, he says, can carry us through a whole life.
prompt: Which good memory from childhood do you carry with you?

text: Therefore, treat not the orphan with harshness, Nor repulse the petitioner (unheard).
context: From Surah Ad-Duha, addressed to the Prophet, who was himself an orphan. Remember what it was to be vulnerable, and treat the vulnerable gently.
prompt: Who comes to you in need, and how do you receive them?

text: In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,—I am rising to the work of a human being.
context: Even an emperor struggled to get out of bed. His answer was to remember what he was for.
prompt: What work, worthy of a human being, is waiting for you today?

text: Let no man think lightly of good, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little.
context: The companion to verse 121. Goodness, too, accumulates drop by drop.
prompt: What small good thing could you add to the pot today?

text: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
context: Character shows in small things first. How we handle little matters predicts how we will handle large ones.
prompt: What small thing deserves more faithfulness from you?

text: Some men have sought to become famous and renowned, thinking that thus they would make themselves secure against their fellow-men.
