context: Fame is usually sought for security. Epicurus asks whether it ever really delivers it.
prompt: What are you hoping recognition will give you?

text: As often as the wavering and unsteady mind goeth forth, so often reining it in, let him bring it under the control of the Self.
context: Meditation is not never wandering; it is coming back, as many times as it takes.
prompt: Can you be patient with your mind each time it wanders?

text: Old age has a great sense of calm and freedom; when the passions relax their hold, then, as Sophocles says, we are freed from the grasp not of one mad master only, but of many.
context: The elderly Cephalus, at the opening of the Republic, finds that age has freed him from the tyranny of his passions.
prompt: What passion would you be glad to be free of?

text: A friend loveth at all times, And a brother is born for adversity.
context: True friendship is constant, and family shows its worth in hard times.
prompt: Who has been there for you in adversity, and do they know it?

text: The more I love humanity in general, the less I love man in particular.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4
context: Zosima recalls a doctor's confession: loving humanity in the abstract is easy; loving the person in front of us is hard.
prompt: Who is the particular person you find hardest to love?

text: Whoever hath been given gentleness, hath been given a good portion, in this world and the next.
context: Gentleness is presented as a gift in itself, one that improves every part of life.
prompt: Where could you be gentler, with others or with yourself?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee; for instance, the activity of one, and the modesty of another, and the liberality of a third, and some other good quality of a fourth.
context: A simple exercise in gratitude: notice the particular virtues of the people around you.
prompt: Name one good quality in each of three people close to you.

text: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.
context: The ethic of non-harm rests on a simple act of imagination: others fear pain and death just as we do.
prompt: Whose fear could you understand better by putting yourself in their place?

text: …He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.
context: A crowd brings a woman accused of adultery, ready to stone her. One sentence disperses them, oldest first.
prompt: Who are you ready to condemn for something you might also have done?

text: No pleasure is in itself evil, but the things which produce certain pleasures entail annoyances many times greater than the pleasures themselves.
context: The problem is never pleasure itself, but what certain pleasures bring along with them.
prompt: Which pleasure brings trouble along with it?

text: For the mind is verily restless, O Krishna; it is impetuous, strong and difficult to bend. I deem it as hard to curb as the wind. … Without doubt, O mighty-armed, the mind is hard to curb and restless; but it may be curbed by constant practice and by dispassion.
context: Arjuna complains that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees, and offers two remedies: practice and letting go.
prompt: What practice could steady your mind, a little each day?

text: He who is of a calm and happy nature will hardly feel the pressure of age, but to him who is of an opposite disposition youth and age are equally a burden.
context: Cephalus again: what makes a life heavy is not age but temperament.
prompt: What in your temperament makes life lighter, or heavier?

text: Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise; And he that shutteth his lips is esteemed as a man of understanding.
context: A wry observation: silence can make anyone look wise. It also gives us time to become a little wiser.
prompt: Where would silence serve you better than speech?

text: Let us be, first and above all, kind, then honest and then let us never forget each other!
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Epilogue, ch. 3
context: The closing scene of the novel. After all its darkness, Dostoevsky ends with a simple order of priorities.
prompt: Who should you make sure never to forget?

text: Woe to every (kind of) scandal-monger and-backbiter, Who pileth up wealth and layeth it by, Thinking that his wealth would make him last for ever!
context: From Surah Al-Humazah. It links two faults, slandering others and hoarding wealth, both rooted in the illusion that we are secure.
prompt: What are you holding onto as if it could make you last forever?

text: Since it is possible that thou mayest depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly.
context: Not a counsel of fear, but of seriousness: live as one who knows life is not guaranteed.
prompt: Which of today's acts would you do differently in that light?

text: Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer thee in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch thee.
context: Harsh speech returns to the speaker. The verse is practical before it is moral.
prompt: What tone have you been using with the people around you?

text: And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.
context: Truth, even uncomfortable truth, is presented as the way to freedom.
prompt: What truth would set you free if you finally faced it?

text: When tolerable security against our fellow-men is attained, then on a basis of power sufficient to afford support and of material prosperity arises in most genuine form the security of a quiet private life withdrawn from the multitude.
context: Epicurus advised his followers to 'live unnoticed', valuing a quiet life among friends over public ambition.
prompt: Where could you choose quiet over attention?

text: Humility, unpretentiousness, harmlessness, forgiveness, rectitude, service of the teacher, purity, steadfastness, self-control.
context: Part of a list of qualities the Gita calls true knowledge. Wisdom shows itself as character.
prompt: Which of these qualities would you like to grow in?

text: The power and capacity of learning exists in the soul already; and that just as the eye was unable to turn from darkness to light without the whole body, so too the instrument of knowledge can only by the movement of the whole soul be turned from the world of becoming into that of being.
context: Education, for Plato, is not pouring knowledge into an empty vessel but turning the whole soul toward the light.
prompt: What understanding is already in you, waiting to be turned toward?

text: He that giveth answer before he heareth, It is folly and confusion unto him.
context: Answering before listening fully is both foolish and embarrassing.
prompt: Who deserves to be heard all the way through before you answer?

text: Above all, avoid falsehood, every kind of falsehood, especially falseness to yourself. Watch over your own deceitfulness and look into it every hour, every minute. Avoid being scornful, both to others and to yourself. What seems to you bad within you will grow purer from the very fact of your observing it in yourself.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 4
context: Zosima's advice: honest self-observation, without scorn, is itself a kind of healing.
prompt: What could you observe in yourself today without scorn?

text: Feed the hungry and visit the sick, and free the captive, if he be unjustly confined. Assist any person oppressed, whether Muslim or non-Muslim.
context: A short list of duties toward others. The final line, in Suhrawardy's collection, extends help to anyone oppressed, of any faith.
prompt: Who near you is hungry, sick or treated unjustly?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Though thou shouldest be going to live three thousand years and as many times ten thousand years, still remember that no man loses any other life than this which he now lives, nor lives any other than this which he now loses.
context: However long a life is, it is only ever lived one present moment at a time, and that moment is all anyone can lose.
prompt: What would it mean to live this moment rather than count your years?

text: A man who has learnt little, grows old like an ox; his flesh grows, but his knowledge does not grow.
context: Growing older is not the same as growing wiser. The body grows on its own; understanding needs tending.
prompt: What have you learned this year that changed you?

text: …Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
context: An image from farming: a seed must be buried and lose its form before it can grow into a harvest.
prompt: What might need to end in your life so that something new can grow?

text: Fortune but seldom interferes with the wise man; his greatest and highest interests have been, are, and will be, directed by reason throughout the course of his life.
context: Luck affects the outer edges of a life. What matters most is guided by our own reasoning.
prompt: What part of your life is governed by reason rather than luck?

text: Harmlessness, truth, absence of wrath, renunciation, peacefulness, absence of crookedness, compassion to living beings, uncovetousness, mildness, modesty, absence of fickleness, vigour, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of envy and pride.
context: From a list of the 'divine qualities' a person can cultivate.
prompt: Which of these is most alive in you, and which least?

text: In heaven, I replied, there is laid up a pattern of it, methinks, which he who desires may behold, and beholding, may set his own house in order.
context: The ideal city may never exist on earth. But anyone can use it as a pattern for ordering their own life.
prompt: What pattern are you ordering your inner house by?

text: It is the discretion of a man to be slow to anger, And it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
context: Patience is called discretion, and overlooking an offence is called glory.
prompt: What offence could you gracefully pass over?

text: Loving humility is marvelously strong, the strongest of all things, and there is nothing else like it.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 3
context: Zosima on humility: not weakness, but the strongest force there is.
prompt: Where could humility be your strength today?

text: The mutual rivalry for piling up (the good things of this world) diverts you (from the more serious things), Until ye visit the graves.
context: Surah At-Takathur ('Rivalry in Increase'). The race to accumulate keeps people distracted their whole lives.
prompt: What competition for 'more' is distracting you from what matters?

text: How much trouble he avoids who does not look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only to what he does himself.
context: Much unrest comes from monitoring others. Marcus turns his attention back to his own conduct.
prompt: Whose life have you been watching instead of tending your own?

text: Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer.
context: Before guiding others, first set oneself on the right course.
prompt: What advice you often give could you take yourself?

text: Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
context: Love measured by sacrifice. Laying down one's life can mean dying, but also giving one's life, day by day, for others.
prompt: For whom are you laying down your life, a little at a time?

text: The just man enjoys the greatest peace of mind, while the unjust is full of the utmost disquietude.
context: For Epicurus, justice is valuable partly because it lets us sleep at night.
prompt: Is there anything on your conscience disturbing your peace?

text: Triple is the gate of this hell, destructive of the self—lust, wrath, and greed; therefore let man renounce these three.
context: Lust, anger and greed are named as the three doors to self-destruction.
prompt: Which of the three doors stands most open in your life?

text: Then to injure a friend or any one else is not the act of a just man, but of the opposite, who is the unjust?
context: Against the common view that justice means helping friends and harming enemies, Socrates argues that a just person harms no one.
prompt: Is there anyone you feel entitled to harm?

text: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out.
context: A person's real purposes lie deep, like water in a well. It takes understanding, and good questions, to draw them up.
prompt: What deep intention in you have you not yet drawn out?

text: Man is fond of reckoning up his troubles, but does not count his joys. If he counted them up as he ought, he would see that every lot has enough happiness provided for it.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground II, ch. 6
context: Spoken by the bitter narrator of Notes from Underground, yet true: we tally our troubles and forget our joys.
prompt: What joys could you count today?

text: What actions are most excellent? To gladden the heart of a human being, to feed the hungry, to help the afflicted, to lighten the sorrow of the sorrowful, and to remove the wrongs of the injured.
context: Asked which deeds are best, the answer is entirely about other people: gladdening, feeding, helping, comforting, setting right.
prompt: Whose heart could you gladden today?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
context: Epictetus does not ask us to stop caring, but to stop demanding that reality match our wishes.
prompt: What would you accept today if you stopped arguing with it?

text: Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord? With self well subdued, a man finds a lord such as few can find.
context: No one else can master our mind for us. Self-reliance is at the heart of the Buddha's teaching.
prompt: Where are you waiting for someone else to change what only you can?

text: …It is more blessed to give than to receive.
context: Paul quotes this saying in a farewell speech. It appears nowhere in the Gospels, so it was likely passed down by word of mouth.
prompt: When did giving last make you happier than receiving?

text: Unlimited time and limited time afford an equal amount of pleasure, if we measure the limits of that pleasure by reason.
context: A complete life is not measured by its length. Understood rightly, a finite life can be whole.
prompt: What would make your life feel complete, regardless of its length?

text: Speech causing no annoyance, truthful, pleasant and beneficial.
context: The Gita describes an 'austerity of speech': words that are true, kind and helpful at once.
prompt: Were your words today truthful, pleasant and beneficial?

text: A State, I said, arises, as I conceive, out of the needs of mankind; no one is self-sufficing, but all of us have many wants.
context: Plato begins his account of society with interdependence. No one is self-sufficient.
prompt: Whom do you depend on that you rarely think about?

text: For a righteous man falleth seven times, and riseth up again, But the wicked stumble under adversity.
context: The righteous are not those who never fall, but those who keep getting up.
prompt: What fall do you need to rise from again?

text: What man wants is simply independent choice, whatever that independence may cost and wherever it may lead.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground I, ch. 7
context: The Underground Man argues that people are not calculating machines: above all, we want to choose for ourselves.
prompt: Where are you choosing freely, and where just following?

text: Know ye (all), that the life of this world is but play and amusement, pomp and mutual boasting and multiplying, (in rivalry) among yourselves, riches and children…
context: The verse goes on to compare worldly life to rain-fed crops that flourish, turn yellow and crumble.
prompt: Which of these 'amusements' takes up most of your attention?

text: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
context: Everything we hold is on loan. Speaking of 'returning' rather than 'losing' changes how we hold what we have while we have it.
prompt: What do you hold that you could hold more lightly, and more gratefully?

text: By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another.
context: Responsibility is personal: no one can do our wrong for us, and no one can make us pure in our place.
prompt: What is yours alone to take responsibility for?

text: Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep.
context: Paul's description of real community: sharing both joy and grief, without envy or distance.
prompt: Whose joy or sorrow could you share today?

text: He who understands the limits of life knows how easy it is to procure enough to remove the pain of want and make the whole of life complete and perfect. Hence he has no longer any need of things which are not to be won save by labour and conflict.
context: Knowing how little we truly need frees us from struggles that were never necessary.
prompt: Which of your struggles is for something you don't really need?

text: Which at first is as venom but in the end is as nectar; that pleasure is said to be pure, born of the blissful knowledge of the Self. That which from the union of the senses with their objects at first is as nectar, but in the end is like venom, that pleasure is accounted passionate.
context: Two kinds of pleasure: one bitter at first and sweet in the end, the other sweet at first and bitter in the end.
prompt: Which of your pleasures are venom first, and which nectar first?

text: The State in which the rulers are most reluctant to govern is always the best and most quietly governed, and the State in which they are most eager, the worst.
context: Those who crave power are often least fit for it.
prompt: Where are you seeking power, and why?

text: A word fitly spoken Is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
context: The right word at the right moment is compared to golden fruit in a silver setting: beautiful because it fits.
prompt: What well-timed word could you offer someone today?

text: Suffering is the sole origin of consciousness. Though I did lay it down at the beginning that consciousness is the greatest misfortune for man, yet I know man prizes it and would not give it up for any satisfaction.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, Notes from Underground I, ch. 9
context: A paradox from the Underground Man: awareness brings pain, yet no one would trade it for comfortable unawareness.
prompt: What has a painful experience made you more aware of?

text: Give the labourer his wage before his perspiration be dry.
context: A saying about fairness in work: pay promptly, while the effort is still fresh.
prompt: Whom do you owe, in money, thanks or recognition, and how soon can you pay it?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you. Stretch out your hand and take a portion with decency. Suppose that it passes by you. Do not detain it.
context: Life passes things around like dishes at a dinner. Take your share with grace; don't grab, and don't cling to what moves on.
prompt: What is passing by you that you are trying to hold onto?

text: Look upon the world as a bubble, look upon it as a mirage: the king of death does not see him who thus looks down upon the world.
context: Seeing the world as a bubble or a mirage is not despair but freedom: what passes cannot hold us.
prompt: What would you stop clinging to if you saw it as a passing bubble?

text: Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.
context: The close of a passage on not repaying evil for evil. Good is not passive; it is the way evil is actually overcome.
prompt: Where could good be your answer to something that wronged you?

text: All such desires as lead to no pain when they remain ungratified are unnecessary, and the longing is easily got rid of, when the thing desired is difficult to procure or when the desires seem likely to produce harm.
context: A test for any desire: would going without it actually hurt? If not, it can be let go.
prompt: Which desire would cost you nothing to give up?

text: Whoso forsaketh all desires and goeth onwards free from yearnings, selfless and without egoism—he goeth to Peace.
context: Peace comes not from getting what we want but from being free of the craving and the ego that drive us.
prompt: What yearning could you set down, even for an hour?

text: He sets in order his own inner life, and is his own master and his own law, and at peace with himself.
context: Plato's definition of justice in the soul: each part doing its own work, in harmony, like notes in a scale.
prompt: What would it take to be at peace with yourself today?

text: Answer not a fool according to his folly, Lest thou also be like unto him. Answer a fool according to his folly, Lest he be wise in his own eyes.
context: Two verses placed side by side that seem to contradict each other. Wisdom lies in knowing which situation you are in.
prompt: When is it wiser to answer, and when to stay silent?

text: Man is but a reed, the most feeble thing in nature; but he is a thinking reed.
context: Perhaps Pascal's most famous line. Human beings are fragile, but our capacity to think gives us a dignity the universe lacks.
prompt: How are you using your thinking today?

text: …But it is possible that ye dislike a thing which is good for you, and that ye love a thing which is bad for you…
context: Our likes and dislikes are poor guides to what is truly good for us.
prompt: What did you once resist that turned out to be good for you?

text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you.
context: Insults wound only when we agree with them inwardly. Epictetus hands the power back to the one being insulted.
prompt: Whose words have you allowed to irritate you, and could you take that permission back?

text: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.
context: Often called the heart of the Buddha's teaching in a single verse: avoid harm, do good, clarify the mind.
prompt: Which of the three do you most need today?

text: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil; Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth; Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.
context: Paul's famous hymn to love. 'Charity' is the King James rendering of the Greek agape: selfless, active love.
prompt: Which line of this describes the love you most want to give?

text: The same conviction which inspires confidence that nothing we have to fear is eternal or even of long duration, also enables us to see that even in our limited conditions of life nothing enhances our security so much as friendship.
context: In an uncertain world, nothing makes us more secure than friends.
prompt: Who makes you feel safe, and do you make them feel the same?

text: Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins. The senses they call the horses, the objects of the senses their roads. … He who has no understanding and whose mind (the reins) is never firmly held, his senses (horses) are unmanageable, like vicious horses of a charioteer. But he who has understanding and whose mind is always firmly held, his senses are under control, like good horses of a charioteer.
context: One of the most famous images in Indian philosophy. The senses are horses; the mind is the reins; understanding is the driver.
prompt: Who is driving your chariot today: the horses or the charioteer?

text: He who is the real tyrant, whatever men may think, is the real slave.
context: The tyrant seems to have everything, but is ruled by desires he can never satisfy.
prompt: Which of your desires rules you more than you rule it?

text: Boast not thyself of to-morrow; For thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
context: Tomorrow is not ours to promise. Humility about the future frees us to attend to today.
prompt: What are you counting on tomorrow that you could act on today?

text: So we never live, but we hope to live; and, as we are always preparing to be happy, it is inevitable we should never be so.
context: We live in memories and plans, rarely in the present. Always preparing to be happy, we never are.
prompt: What are you postponing being happy about?

text: The whole goat remaineth except its shoulder; that is, that remaineth which ye have given away, and what ye have kept in the house is frail.
context: A goat was slaughtered and most of it given to the poor and neighbours, leaving only a shoulder. The Prophet replied that what was given away is what remains.
prompt: What have you given away that remains with you?
translation: Abdullah al-Mamun al-Suhrawardy, The Sayings of Muhammad (1905)

text: It is a mark of a mean capacity to spend much time on the things which concern the body, such as much exercise, much eating, much drinking, much easing of the body, much copulation. But these things should be done as subordinate things; and let all your care be directed to the mind.
context: Epictetus does not despise the body, but asks us to keep its care in proportion, and to give our best attention to the mind.
prompt: How much of your attention goes to tending your inner life?

text: Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred!
context: From the chapter on happiness. Happiness here is not the absence of hostility, but freedom from returning it.
prompt: What would it feel like to live free from hatred, even toward one person?

text: When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
context: Growth means letting go of old ways of thinking, not just adding new ones.
prompt: What childish thing are you ready to put away?

text: Of our desires some are natural and necessary; others are natural, but not necessary; others, again, are neither natural nor necessary, but are due to illusory opinion.
context: Epicurus' famous threefold sorting of desires. An ancient commentator gives examples: drink when thirsty; fine food; crowns and statues in one's honour.
prompt: Sort three of your current desires into these three kinds.

text: Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard.
context: A call to wakefulness. The path to self-knowledge is as narrow as a razor's edge, which is exactly why it needs attention.
prompt: What are you being called to wake up to?

text: No man would keep his hands off what was not his own when he could safely take what he liked…
context: From the story of the Ring of Gyges, which makes its wearer invisible. Glaucon challenges Socrates: would anyone stay just if no one could see?
prompt: What would you do differently if no one could ever see?

text: Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; A stranger, and not thine own lips.
context: Praise means more when it comes from others. Self-praise tends to empty itself.
prompt: Could you let your work speak for itself today?

text: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
context: Pascal, a brilliant mathematician, insisted that not all knowing is logical. Some truths are felt before they are proven.
prompt: What does your heart know that your reason can't explain?

text: …Every soul draws the meed of its acts on none but itself: no bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another…
context: A statement of personal responsibility: each person answers for their own deeds.
prompt: What burden are you carrying that isn't yours, or avoiding that is?

text: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty. It is not possible then for him to follow that which seems right to you, but that which seems right to himself. … you will be mild in temper to him who reviles you; for say on each occasion, It seemed so to him.
context: People act on what seems right to them. Remembering this softens anger without excusing the act.
prompt: Who has acted on how things seemed to them, and can you see it from there?

text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.
context: Every victory creates a loser, and the loser's bitterness. Contentment lies beyond the game of winning and losing.
prompt: Where are you trying to win when you could simply let go?

text: For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face…
context: Ancient mirrors were polished metal and gave a dim, distorted image. Our understanding now, Paul says, is partial.
prompt: Where might you be seeing only part of the picture?

text: On this blissful day, which is also the last of my life, I write this to you. My continual sufferings from strangury and dysentery are so great that nothing could augment them; but over against them all I set gladness of mind at the remembrance of our past conversations.
context: Written by Epicurus on the day he died, in great pain. Memories of friendship and conversation outweighed everything else.
prompt: Which conversations would you want to remember at the end?

text: Fools dwelling in darkness, wise in their own conceit, and puffed up with vain knowledge, go round and round, staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind…
context: Death warns Nachiketas about people who mistake cleverness for wisdom.
prompt: Whom are you following, and can they see the way?

text: Human nature was originally one and we were a whole, and the desire and pursuit of the whole is called love.
context: From Aristophanes' speech: humans were once whole beings, split in two, and love is the longing to be whole again.
prompt: What makes you feel whole?

text: Iron sharpeneth iron; So a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
context: Good friends sharpen each other, sometimes through friction.
prompt: Who sharpens you, and whom do you sharpen?

text: Man is neither angel nor brute, and the unfortunate thing is that he who would act the angel acts the brute.
context: Trying to be more than human often makes us less. Pascal warns against spiritual pride.
prompt: Where are you trying to be an angel instead of a human?

text: That man can have nothing but what he strives for.
context: From Surah An-Najm. Effort, not wishing, shapes what a person comes to have.
prompt: What are you striving for, and is it what you truly want?

text: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of the act by that handle wherein he acts unjustly, for this is the handle which cannot be borne; but lay hold of the other, that he is your brother.
context: Every situation can be picked up in a way that can be carried or a way that cannot. We choose the handle.
prompt: Which handle are you holding a difficult relationship by?

text: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.
context: A list of what truly counts as wealth. Nirvana is the Buddhist name for the final peace beyond craving.
prompt: By this measure, how rich are you today?

text: …whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
context: A farming image of consequence: what we plant through our choices is what we will harvest.
prompt: What are you sowing now that you will want to reap later?

text:
The nations wax, the nations wane away;
In a brief space the generations pass,
And like to runners hand the lamp of life
One unto other.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius pictures the generations as relay runners, each handing the torch of life to the next.
prompt: What are you carrying that you hope to hand on?

text: The Self-existent pierced the openings (of the senses) so that they turn forward; therefore man looks forward, not backward into himself. Some wise man, however, with his eyes closed and wishing for immortality, saw the Self behind.
context: Our senses face outward, so we naturally look outward. The Upanishad invites the rarer turn inward.
prompt: What would you see if you closed your eyes and looked within?

text: “This, my dear Socrates,” said the stranger of Mantineia, “is that life above all others which man should live, in the contemplation of beauty absolute.”
context: The priestess Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from beautiful bodies to beautiful souls, ideas, and finally beauty itself.
prompt: Where did you notice beauty today?

text: That which hath been is that which shall be, And that which hath been done is that which shall be done; And there is nothing new under the sun.
context: Kohelet observes that human life moves in cycles. What feels unprecedented has usually been lived before.
prompt: What struggle of yours have countless others already lived through?

text: The only thing which consoles us for our miseries is diversion, and yet this is the greatest of our miseries. For it is this which principally hinders us from reflecting upon ourselves, and which makes us insensibly ruin ourselves.
context: Pascal saw distraction as both comfort and trap: it keeps us from reflecting on our lives. (A typo in the source edition, 'it' for 'is', is corrected here.)
prompt: What distraction keeps you from reflecting on your life?

text: Then shall anyone who has done an atom's weight of good, see it! And anyone who has done an atom's weight of evil, shall see it.
context: The closing verses of Surah Az-Zalzalah. Nothing we do is too small to matter.
prompt: What atom's weight of good could you do today?

text: If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write.
context: From a discourse on how habits are formed: every capacity is strengthened by its corresponding action, and weakened by neglect.
prompt: What do you want to become, and did you practise it today?

text: He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins.
context: Anger is pictured as a runaway chariot. The real driver is the one who can stop it.
prompt: When did you last hold back anger, and how did it feel afterwards?

text: …let not the sun go down upon your wrath.
context: Anger itself is not condemned here, but anger left to settle overnight. Resolve it before the day ends.
prompt: Is there anger you could resolve before the sun goes down today?

text:
And in fee-simple life is given to none,
But unto all mere usufruct. Look back:
Nothing to us was all fore-passed eld
Of time the eternal, ere we had a birth.
And Nature holds this like a mirror up
Of time-to-be when we are dead and gone.
And what is there so horrible appears?
Now what is there so sad about it all?
Is't not serener far than any sleep?
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Life is lent, not owned. And the eternity after death, Lucretius argues, is no more frightening than the eternity before birth.
prompt: If life is on loan, how do you want to use it?

text: The true prevails, not the untrue; by the true the path is laid out.
context: The first words, 'Satyameva jayate', are India's national motto.
prompt: Where do you need to trust that truth will prevail?

text: For wisdom is a most beautiful thing, and Love is of the beautiful; and therefore Love is also a philosopher or lover of wisdom, and being a lover of wisdom is in a mean between the wise and the ignorant.
context: Love, in Diotima's account, is neither wise nor ignorant but always reaching: the very definition of a philosopher.
prompt: What are you reaching for that you don't yet have?

text: Better is a handful of quietness, Than both the hands full of labour and striving after wind.
context: One hand full of quiet is better than two hands full of toil. Kohelet questions the endless pursuit of more.
prompt: What would a handful of quietness look like today?

text: How comes it that a cripple does not offend us, but that a fool does? Because a cripple recognises that we walk straight, whereas a fool declares that it is we who are silly; if it were not so, we should feel pity and not anger.
context: We are angered not by others' limitations but by their claim that we are the ones who are wrong.
prompt: Whose disagreement angers you, and why does it sting?

text: Is there any Reward for Good - other than Good?
context: A rhetorical question from Surah Ar-Rahman. Goodness calls for goodness in return.
prompt: Whose goodness to you have you not yet returned?

text: What is the first business of him who philosophizes? To throw away self-conceit. For it is impossible for a man to begin to learn that which he thinks that he knows.
context: Learning begins with humility. Whatever we think we already understand, we stop examining.
prompt: What do you think you already know that might be worth relearning?

text: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
context: Each quality is overcome by its opposite: anger by love, evil by good, greed by generosity, lies by truth.
prompt: Which opposite does a situation in your life call for?

text: …whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.
context: Written by Paul from prison. What we dwell on shapes our inner life, so he asks his readers to choose what they dwell on.
prompt: What lovely or true thing could you dwell on today?

text:
The man who sickens of his home goes out,
Forth from his splendid halls, and straight—returns,
Feeling i'faith no better off abroad.
He races, driving his Gallic ponies along,
Down to his villa, madly,—as in haste
To hurry help to a house afire.—At once
He yawns, as soon as foot has touched the threshold,
Or drowsily goes off in sleep and seeks
Forgetfulness, or maybe bustles about
And makes for town again. In such a way
Each human flees himself—a self in sooth,
As happens, he by no means can escape;
And willy-nilly he cleaves to it and loathes,
Sick, sick, and guessing not the cause of ail.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: A strikingly modern portrait of restlessness: the rich man rushing to his country house, bored on arrival, rushing back to town, always fleeing himself.
prompt: What are you running from by keeping busy?

text: Two birds, inseparable friends, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating…
context: One bird tastes the fruits of life, sweet and bitter; the other simply watches. Many read them as two sides of ourselves: the one who experiences and the one who witnesses.
prompt: Can you be, for a moment, the bird that only watches?

text: Give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one. May I reckon the wise to be the wealthy, and may I have such a quantity of gold as a temperate man and he only can bear and carry.
context: Socrates' prayer at the end of the Phaedrus: inner beauty, harmony between inner and outer life, and only as much wealth as a temperate person can carry.
prompt: How could your outward life better match your inward one?

text: Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth, and hath not another to lift him up.
context: A reflection on companionship: two people can lift each other in ways no one can alone.
prompt: Who lifts you up, and whom could you lift?

text: A mere trifle consoles us, for a mere trifle distresses us.
context: Pascal on the fragility of our moods: small things lift us because small things also bring us down.
prompt: What trifle upset you recently, and what trifle could lift you?

text: And when they hear vain talk, they turn away therefrom and say: "To us our deeds, and to you yours; peace be to you: we seek not the ignorant."
context: A description of how the dignified respond to idle or provocative talk: not with argument, but with peace and distance.
prompt: Which conversation could you leave with a simple 'peace be to you'?

text: So if you wish for your son or friend when it is not allowed to you, you must know that you are wishing for a fig in winter.
context: A hard but tender image: the people we love are given to us for a season, like fruit. Wishing them permanent is wishing for figs in winter.
prompt: Who is in season in your life right now, and how will you enjoy them?

text: This is an old saying, O Atula, this is not only of to-day: ‘They blame him who sits silent, they blame him who speaks much, they also blame him who says little; there is no one on earth who is not blamed.' There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised.
context: Addressed to a disciple named Atula. Whatever we do, someone will criticise it; whatever we do, someone will praise it.
prompt: Whose criticism have you been trying to avoid at the cost of being yourself?

text: …for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
context: Also written in prison. Paul presents contentment not as a mood but as something learned.
prompt: What would help you learn contentment where you are now?

text:
Why not,
Even like a banqueter, depart the halls,
Laden with life? why not with mind content
Take now, thou fool, thy unafflicted rest?
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Nature speaks to someone afraid of dying: if your life has been good, why not leave it like a guest who has dined well?
prompt: What would it mean to feel 'laden with life'?

text: And he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it. When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?
context: The Isha Upanishad's vision of unity: when we see ourselves in others and others in ourselves, the walls that cause sorrow fall away.
prompt: Whom could you see as part of yourself today?

text: Let the figure be composite—a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. … the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him.
context: Plato's image of the soul as a charioteer with two horses, one noble and one unruly. Reason must steer both.
prompt: Which of your horses has been pulling harder lately?

text: Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof; And the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
context: Endings reveal what beginnings only promise, and patience outlasts pride.
prompt: What are you rushing that would benefit from patience?

text: Curiosity is only vanity. Most frequently we wish to know but to talk.
context: A sharp observation: much of what we want to know, we want to know in order to tell others.
prompt: What would you still want to experience if you could never tell anyone?

text: …If a wicked person comes to you with any news, ascertain the truth, lest ye harm people unwittingly, and afterwards become full of repentance for what ye have done.
context: From Surah Al-Hujurat, a chapter of social ethics. Verify before you act on news, especially news about other people.
prompt: What have you believed about someone without checking?

text: Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 2
context: Seneca's whole argument in one line: the problem is not the length of life but how we spend it.
prompt: What would 'using it well' look like this week?

text: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.
context: Purifying silver takes patient, repeated work. So does refining one's character.
prompt: What small impurity could you work on, little by little?

text: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
context: A short instruction for discernment: test everything, then keep what proves good.
prompt: Which belief of yours have you never really tested?

text:
Those tortures said to be
In Acheron, the deep, they all are ours
Here in this life.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Lucretius reads the myths of the underworld as pictures of our own anxieties, which we suffer now, not after death.
prompt: Which torment of yours lives only in your mind?

text: When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any man!
context: A paradox at the opening of the Isha Upanishad: we enjoy most fully what we no longer try to possess.
prompt: What could you enjoy more by holding it less tightly?

text: This discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves. The specific which you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence, and you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth; they will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing.
context: An Egyptian king warns the inventor of writing that it will weaken memory and give only the appearance of wisdom. The worry sounds familiar today.
prompt: What do you know only because it is stored somewhere, not in you?

text: Say not thou: ‘How was it that the former days were better than these?’ for it is not out of wisdom that thou inquirest concerning this.
context: Nostalgia can be a way of avoiding the present. Kohelet calls the question itself unwise.
prompt: What good thing about these days are you overlooking?

text: Cleopatra's nose: had it been shorter, the whole aspect of the world would have been altered.
context: History, and our own lives, turn on tiny details. Small causes can have enormous effects.
prompt: What small thing changed the course of your life?

text: …Avoid suspicion as much (as possible): for suspicion in some cases is a sin: And spy not on each other behind their backs…
context: The same chapter continues: suspicion, spying and backbiting corrode a community from within.
prompt: Whom have you been suspicious of without real cause?

text: You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3
context: Seneca names a strange contradiction: we are anxious because we are mortal, yet we behave as if we had all the time in the world.
prompt: Which of your desires assumes you will live forever?

text: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler.
context: Our own faults are hidden from us in a way others' are not. The verse goes on to compare this to a cheat hiding a bad throw of the dice.
prompt: What fault of yours might be obvious to others but hidden from you?

text: …For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.
context: Said to people confidently planning their next year of business. Life is like morning mist: real, and brief.
prompt: If your life is a vapour, what do you want it to carry?

text:
O wretched minds of men! O blinded hearts!
In how great perils, in what darks of life
Are spent the human years, however brief!—
O not to see that nature for herself
Barks after nothing, save that pain keep off,
Disjoined from the body, and that mind enjoy
Delightsome feeling, far from care and fear!
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things II
context: Lucretius laments how people waste their short lives striving for power, when nature asks only for freedom from pain and a mind at ease.
prompt: What does your nature actually ask of you today?

text: Here also, in this body, forsooth, you do not perceive the True (Sat), my son; but there indeed it is. That which is the subtile essence, in it all that exists has its self. It is the True. It is the Self, and thou, O Svetaketu, art it.
context: A father teaches his son Svetaketu by dissolving salt in water: invisible, yet present in every sip. 'Thou art that' (tat tvam asi) is one of the great sayings of the Upanishads.
prompt: What is present in your life even though you cannot see it?

text: How singular is the thing called pleasure, and how curiously related to pain, which might be thought to be the opposite of it; for they are never present to a man at the same instant, and yet he who pursues either is generally compelled to take the other; their bodies are two, but they are joined by a single head.
context: Socrates, his chains just removed on the day of his death, rubs his leg and reflects on how pleasure and pain always follow each other.
prompt: Which pleasure in your life always seems to bring its pain?

text: Whatsoever thy hand attaineth to do by thy strength, that do; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
context: Because life is finite, whatever we can do, we should do with our full strength now.
prompt: What deserves your full strength today?

text: It is not from space that I must seek my dignity, but from the government of my thought.
context: Our dignity lies not in what we possess or how much room we occupy, but in how we govern our minds.
prompt: How well are you governing your thoughts?

text: …Why say ye that which ye do not?
context: A pointed question about the gap between words and deeds.
prompt: What have you said you would do, and not yet done?

text: How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it!
source: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life 3
context: Said of people who plan to start living once they retire. Seneca's point: there is no later version of life waiting for you.
prompt: What have you been saving for 'someday'?

text: A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned.
context: Real learning shows in character (patience, freedom from fear and hatred), not in how much one talks.
prompt: Where could you speak less and understand more?

text: …Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.
context: Perhaps the most demanding line of the Sermon on the Mount: love that extends even to those who wish us harm.
prompt: What would one small act of goodwill toward a difficult person look like?

text:
Since from amid the well-spring of delights
Bubbles some drop of bitter to torment
Among the very flowers…
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things IV
context: Even in the middle of pleasure, something bitter rises, often regret or unease of the mind.
prompt: What bitterness rises in you even amid good things?

text: The Infinite (bhûman) is bliss. There is no bliss in anything finite. Infinity only is bliss.
context: The sage Sanatkumara teaches that no finite thing can bring lasting joy.
prompt: What finite thing have you been expecting to make you whole?

text: Lest we become misologists, he replied, no worse thing can happen to a man than this. For as there are misanthropists or haters of men, there are also misologists or haters of ideas, and both spring from the same cause, which is ignorance of the world.
context: After an argument collapses, Socrates warns against giving up on reasoning altogether, just as disappointment can turn people against humanity.
prompt: Where has disappointment made you cynical?

text: …the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
context: Kohelet notices that talent does not guarantee success. Time and chance play their part in every life.
prompt: How might you hold your successes, and failures, more humbly?

text: Let us endeavour, then, to think well; this is the principle of morality.
context: Pascal concludes that since thought is our dignity, thinking well is where ethics begins.
prompt: Where would better thinking lead to better living?

text: Hold to forgiveness; command what is right; But turn away from the ignorant.
context: Three short commands often described as a summary of good character.
prompt: Which of the three is hardest for you right now?

text: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it: if it delays, it will come to an end.
context: Seneca's treatise on anger is a manual for a calmer life. His first remedy is the simplest: wait.
prompt: When did waiting before you reacted last save you from regret?

text: You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers. The thoughtful who enter the way are freed from the bondage of Mara.
context: Even the Buddhas can only point the way. Tathagata is a title of the Buddha; Mara stands for the forces of delusion.
prompt: What effort is yours to make that no teacher can make for you?

text: …Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth!
context: James compares the tongue to a small spark that sets a whole forest alight.
prompt: What small word could start a fire, or put one out, today?

text:
But rather this:
To look on all things with a master eye
And mind at peace.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things V
context: Lucretius contrasts anxious rituals with what he sees as true reverence: looking on the world with calm and clarity.
prompt: What would you see differently if you looked with a mind at peace?

text: I have heard from men like you, that he who knows the Self overcomes grief. I am in grief. Do, Sir, help me over this grief of mine.
context: The learned Narada has mastered every science, yet comes to his teacher in grief. Knowledge of things, he discovers, is not knowledge of oneself.
prompt: What do you know about the world that you have not yet learned about yourself?

text: Is not philosophy the practice of death?
context: For Plato, philosophy loosens our attachment to the body and its fears, a lifelong rehearsal for letting go.
prompt: What would you practise letting go of today?

text: Cast thy bread upon the waters, For thou shalt find it after many days.
context: Often read as a call to generosity: give freely, without calculating the return, and good tends to come back.
prompt: Where could you give without expecting anything back?

text: “I did that,” says my memory. “I could not have done that,” says my pride, and remains inexorable. Eventually—the memory yields.
source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil 68
context: A two-line portrait of self-deception: when memory and pride disagree, pride usually wins.
prompt: What has your pride persuaded your memory to forget?

text: Truly man was created very impatient;- Fretful when evil touches him; And niggardly when good reaches him.
context: An honest portrait of human nature: anxious in hardship and grasping in comfort. The verses that follow describe those who rise above it.
prompt: Do you recognise yourself in this, and in which moments?

text: Whoever recalls to his mind how often he himself has been the victim of undeserved suspicion, how often fortune has given his true service an appearance of wrong-doing, how many persons he has begun by hating and ended by loving, will be able to keep himself from becoming angry straightway.
context: Remembering our own experience of being misjudged makes us slower to misjudge others.
prompt: Who did you once dislike and later come to love?

text: Through zeal knowledge is gotten, through lack of zeal knowledge is lost; let a man who knows this double path of gain and loss thus place himself that knowledge may grow.
context: Knowledge grows with effort and fades without it. The wise place themselves where it can grow.
prompt: Where could you put yourself so that your understanding grows?

text: My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.
context: Love is proven in action, not declared in words.
prompt: How could you show love today rather than say it?

text:
Therefore death to us
Is nothing, nor concerns us in the least.
source: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things III
context: Lucretius restates Epicurus in verse, at the heart of his long argument against the fear of death.
prompt: How much of your life is shaped by a fear of its ending?

text: He is not born, nor doth he die; nor having been, ceaseth he any more to be; unborn, perpetual, eternal and ancient, he is not slain when the body is slaughtered.
context: Krishna speaks of the innermost self, which the Gita holds to be untouched by birth and death.
prompt: What in you feels unchanged since you were a child?

text: Of all the men of his time whom I have known, he was the wisest and justest and best.
context: The last line of the Phaedo, Phaedo's tribute to Socrates after his death.
prompt: What would you want those who knew you to say?

text: He that observeth the wind shall not sow; And he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.
context: The farmer who waits for perfect conditions never plants. Waiting for certainty can become a way of never starting.
prompt: What are you not sowing because you are watching the wind?

text: Every day and every hour, every minute, walk round yourself and watch yourself, and see that your image is a seemly one.
source: Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov, Book VI, ch. 3
context: Zosima's counsel to watch how we carry ourselves, because others, especially children, are always watching.
prompt: How do you appear to those who look up to you?

text: And cover not Truth with falsehood, nor conceal the Truth when ye know (what it is).
context: Two ways of betraying truth: mixing it with falsehood, and keeping silent when we know it.
prompt: Where are you covering a truth, or keeping it hidden?

text: It is the part of a great mind to despise wrongs done to it; the most contemptuous form of revenge is not to deem one’s adversary worth taking vengeance upon.
context: From Seneca's treatise on anger. Not every slight deserves a response; some are best left beneath notice.
prompt: Which small injury could you let pass without comment?

text: If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great.
context: A simple trade: give up a lesser pleasure for a greater, more lasting one.
prompt: What small pleasure stands between you and a greater one?

text: And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted.
context: A reversal that runs through the Gospels: those who grasp at importance lose it; those who serve find it.
prompt: Where are you trying to exalt yourself, and what would humility look like there?

text: In the morning sow thy seed, And in the evening withhold not thy hand; For thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that, Or whether they both shall be alike good.
context: We cannot know which of our efforts will bear fruit, so we keep sowing, morning and evening.
prompt: What seeds could you keep sowing, without knowing which will grow?

text: Kind words and the covering of faults are better than charity followed by injury…
context: Generosity that humiliates its receiver does more harm than good. A kind word and discretion are worth more.
prompt: Whose faults could you cover with kindness today?
